content: Sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) is a treatment approach for allergic rhinitis, a condition that can significantly affect a person's quality of life. Unlike traditional immunotherapy administered via injection, which carries a risk of severe systemic adverse reactions, SLIT offers a safer alternative by delivering allergens under the tongue. The primary objective of this study was to assess the efficacy and safety of SLIT in both adults and children with allergic rhinitis. To achieve this, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane ENT Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, and others, for randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials. The most recent search was completed on August 14, 2009. The inclusion criteria for the review required studies to focus on SLIT in allergic rhinitis patients, with primary outcomes measured in terms of symptom scores and medication use. Adverse event data were also collected. A total of 60 randomized controlled trials were included in the review, with 49 of these trials suitable for meta-analysis. These trials involved 2333 participants receiving SLIT and 2256 participants receiving a placebo. The analysis revealed that SLIT significantly reduced both symptoms and the need for medication compared to placebo. Specifically, the standardized mean difference (SMD) for symptom reduction was -0.49 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.64 to -0.34, P < 0.00001), while the SMD for reduced medication use was -0.32 (95% CI: -0.43 to -0.21, P < 0.00001). Importantly, none of the trials reported severe systemic reactions or anaphylaxis, and no systemic reactions required the use of adrenaline. The authors concluded that this updated review supports the findings of the original 2003 Cochrane Review. SLIT is an effective treatment for allergic rhinitis and has been demonstrated to be a safe method of administration.
